sites.name: Rosh Hanikra Grottoes
sites.description: Wave-carved white chalk grottoes at Israel's border with Lebanon, the very northern tip of the country's coastline, dived inside the calm inner pool of the Rosh Hanikra visitor park rather than in the open sea. Because this stretch of coast sits right against a sensitive land border, diving requires prior IDF Navy clearance and must be done with a certified local instructor rather than independently. Winter brings the most dramatic wave action against the cliffs above the surface, but the shallow inner pool itself stays calm and forgiving for diving year-round -- the draw here is the eroded limestone tunnels and caves themselves, not depth or current.
sites.pro_tip: Diving requires IDF Navy clearance arranged through a certified local instructor -- this isn't a walk-in shore dive like the sites further south, so book through a Nahariya-area dive club well in advance.

sites.name: Achziv Canyon
sites.description: A long north-south underwater wall about 1km off Achziv National Park, between Nahariya and Rosh Hanikra, boat-accessible only through local dive clubs. Large stony corals over 2m across grow along the wall, with octopus, squid, small rays and the occasional sea turtle patrolling the base. As with Rosh Hanikra further north, IDF Navy permission applies to parts of this stretch of coast, so trips are arranged through operators rather than independently.
sites.pro_tip: Conditions here are most reliable in autumn and winter, when Israel's Mediterranean visibility is at its best for the year -- summer's warmer water brings more algae growth and softer viz.

sites.name: Dor-Habonim Marine Reserve
sites.description: Israel's main Mediterranean marine nature reserve, protecting a stretch of wave-eroded kurkar sandstone coves, ridges and inlets between Dor and Habonim -- calm, shallow, shore-accessible snorkeling and easy diving rather than a boat site. Landmarks along the reserve's coastal trail include the 'Blue Cave' and Shell Bay, and fishing is banned inside the reserve boundary, which has let resident fish -- including large, otherwise heavily fished groupers -- grow bigger and stick around longer than on unprotected stretches of coast.
sites.pro_tip: From Shell Bay, swim about 30m out to find the wreck of an unidentified small freighter that ran aground carrying a cargo of cement roughly 90 years ago -- it now sits in just 2.5m of water and has grown into its own mini artificial reef.

sites.name: Caesarea Underwater Archaeological Park
sites.description: The world's first underwater archaeological park, laid out across the submerged remains of Herod the Great's ancient harbor of Sebastos -- sunken breakwaters, ashlar and concrete blocks, ancient anchors, fallen columns and the wreck of a more recent steamer, spread across several marked, buoyed guided tracks (A-D) ranging from a shallow snorkel-friendly inner basin to deeper reef-wall sections with small caves and tunnels. Run by Old Caesarea Diving Center, based inside Caesarea National Park.
sites.pro_tip: Track A's inner and middle basin tops out around 4m and is snorkel-friendly for less confident swimmers, but ask for Track C or the Cave Reef route if you want to actually see the fallen granite and marble columns from Herod's harbor works.

sites.name: Hadera Power Station Shark Aggregation
sites.description: Not a reef or wreck dive but Israel's single most distinctive Mediterranean marine phenomenon -- the warm-water outflow from the Orot Rabin power station draws large seasonal aggregations of sandbar sharks, with some dusky sharks, into shallow, shore-accessible water. It is a shallow shore/surface observation site rather than a conventional boat dive, and the gathering has been studied continuously since 2016 by University of Haifa researchers tagging and sampling the sharks. Following a fatal shark attack on a diver here in November 2025, Israel's Nature and Parks Authority has actively discouraged entering the water with the sharks, so treat this as a site to watch and understand from a respectful distance rather than a dive to plan.
sites.pro_tip: The sharks cluster tightest right where the warm discharge plume meets the sea, roughly November through the winter into spring -- but check current Nature and Parks Authority guidance before going, since safety rules here have tightened since the 2025 attack and can change season to season.

sites.name: Tel Aviv Reef (Gordon / Bird Head Canyon)
sites.description: The kurkar sandstone reef running along central Tel Aviv's shoreline off Gordon Beach, riddled with natural tunnels, small caves and canyons -- including the Bird Head Canyon off neighbouring Mezizim Beach, named for a bird sculpture onshore used as a surface landmark. Octopus, crabs, lobster, soldierfish and other rocky-reef life shelter in the crevices right in the middle of the city.
sites.pro_tip: Use the bird statue on the Mezizim Beach shorefront as your surface bearing for the Bird Head Canyon entrance -- the crack runs east to west through the reef and is easy to swim past without noticing from the wrong angle.

sites.name: Jaffa Peanut Wreck
sites.description: The wreck of a 1934 Egyptian steamer that sank just off old Jaffa port while carrying a cargo of peanuts, giving the site its enduring nickname. Reachable directly from the beach without a boat, with the boilers, engine block and much of the lower hull still recognizable under a covering of marine growth -- one of the most accessible historic wrecks anywhere on Israel's coast.
sites.pro_tip: Head for the boiler and engine block first -- they're the most intact, easiest-to-identify parts of the wreck, since large sections of the outer hull plating have long since broken down and scattered.

sites.name: Palmachim
sites.description: A shallow, easy shore dive on a rocky reef inside Palmachim Beach National Park, with two small ancient barge wrecks close enough together to combine in a single dive. Crabs, worms, octopus and squid shelter in the reef's crevices, and stingrays and guitarfish are occasional visitors over the sandy patches nearby.
sites.pro_tip: The two barge wrecks sit close enough to each other that a single dive can cover both -- a good low-key option on a day when wind rules out the more exposed northern sites.

sites.name: Elisha Wreck
sites.description: A wreck on a sandy seabed a short boat ride west of Ashdod's Blue Marina, its highest structure at around 12-14m and the surrounding sand closer to 33m -- a deeper boat dive for certified, experienced divers rather than a shore or beginner site.

species.description: The Mediterranean's largest and most iconic reef fish, known locally by its old name 'Lucerna' -- a heavily protected species that all but vanished from open coastline through the 20th century under spearfishing pressure and now survives mainly inside no-take marine reserves and other sheltered, low-disturbance sites.
species.habitat: Rocky reefs, caves and harbor ruins
species.population_info: Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List after population declines exceeding 50% across the Mediterranean during the 20th century from spearfishing and commercial fishing; protected under Israeli and EU law, with reserves like Dor-Habonim among the few places large adults reliably persist.

species.description: Every winter, large numbers of sandbar sharks -- alongside some dusky sharks -- gather in the shallow, warm water discharged by the Orot Rabin power station at Hadera, in one of the most easily observed shark aggregations anywhere in the world; the phenomenon has been studied by University of Haifa researchers since 2016 through tagging, satellite telemetry and blood sampling.
species.habitat: Shallow coastal water, notably power-station warm-water outflows
species.population_info: Globally assessed as Vulnerable, but classified as Endangered specifically within the Mediterranean Sea, where the regional population is considered depleted and declining from historic overfishing; slow growth and low reproductive rate make recovery slow.

species.description: A larger, uniformly mottled-brown relative of the moray eels already logged in the Red Sea catalog -- a distinct Mediterranean species that spends most daylight hours wedged into rock crevices, emerging at night to hunt fish, crustaceans and octopus.
species.population_info: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List with a stable population across its Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic range, though coastal development and habitat loss are watched as ongoing local pressures.

species.description: The Mediterranean's common octopus -- a different species from the Red Sea's Common Reef Octopus already in this catalog -- a master of near-instant camouflage found across rocky and sandy stretches of Israel's coast, from harbor ruins to open reef.
species.population_info: Least Concern and abundant across the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic; short-lived (1-2 years) and fast-growing, with populations that can fluctuate significantly season to season.

species.description: Israel's Mediterranean cuttlefish -- a different species from the Red Sea's Pharaoh Cuttlefish already in this catalog -- hovers over sand and rock with the same near-instant colour-shifting camouflage and W-shaped pupil, spending spring and summer in shallow coastal water before moving to deeper water in autumn and winter.
species.population_info: Least Concern; heavily fished commercially across the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic but with no evidence of range-wide decline, unlike some other regional cephalopod stocks.

species.description: The most common sea turtle in the Mediterranean and the only one that nests in real numbers on Israel's coast -- rounder-headed and more reddish-brown than the Red Sea's hawksbill and green turtles already in this catalog, foraging over open sand and rock and coming ashore at night through the summer to lay eggs on undeveloped stretches of beach.
species.habitat: Open coastal water and nesting beaches
species.population_info: Vulnerable globally, though the separately assessed Mediterranean subpopulation is considered comparatively more stable thanks to decades of nest protection; roughly 170 loggerheads produced an estimated 449 nests along Israel's Mediterranean coast in 2021, a fraction of the roughly 200 nests recorded on just 15km of northern coastline in the 1950s.

species.description: One of the rarest marine mammals on Earth and functionally absent from Israel for half a century before returning as an occasional visitor -- individual seals, most famously an adult female nicknamed 'Yulia' photographed resting on a Tel Aviv-area beach in 2023, have been documented more than 90 times along the coast between Ashkelon and Rosh Hanikra since 2010. A sighting anywhere in these waters remains an exceptional stroke of luck, not something to plan a dive around.
species.habitat: Rocky coastline, sea caves and open water
species.population_info: Critically Endangered, with a total world population estimated at only a few hundred individuals; Israel sits at the eastern edge of a slowly recovering range still centered mainly on Greece, Turkey and the Aegean, and resident breeding on Israeli shores has not been confirmed.

species.description: A Red Sea rabbitfish first recorded on this coast back in 1924 -- one of the earliest and most successful Lessepsian migrants to reach the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal, now one of the most numerous herbivorous fish on Israel's rocky reefs, grazing algae in tight schools. Not a native Mediterranean species: its presence here is a direct result of the Suez Canal connecting the two seas.
species.population_info: Least Concern; genetic studies show continuous, ongoing immigration from the Red Sea rather than a one-off founder population, and it now makes up a large share of the herbivorous fish biomass on shallow Eastern Mediterranean reefs.

species.description: The Marbled Spinefoot's close relative and fellow Lessepsian migrant, first recorded in the Mediterranean in 1956 and now well established alongside it along Israel's coast -- darker and more uniformly olive-brown, without the marbled patterning of S. rivulatus. Also a Red Sea native rather than a true Mediterranean species.
species.population_info: Least Concern; alongside S. rivulatus it has been directly implicated in creating algae-stripped 'barrens' on rocky reefs further north in the Mediterranean, though Israeli reefs -- within its long-established range -- show less of this effect than more recently colonized areas like the Aegean.

species.description: A native Mediterranean seabream easily recognized by the gold stripes running down its silvery body, grazing algae and seagrass in loose schools over shallow rock and Posidonia meadows. Eaten in Israel as well as France and Tunisia, but notorious elsewhere for triggering vivid, temporary hallucinations in anyone who eats a fish that has fed heavily on certain toxic algae -- a genuinely documented, if rare, effect.
species.population_info: Least Concern and widespread and common throughout the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic.
